representations.text:
Your March 30–April 12 records largely match your preceding 28 days, with no sustained shift in sleep or heart measures. Sleep averaged 471 versus 470 minutes, starting around 22:49 and ending consistently at 07:00. Weekend sleep averaged 468 versus 472 minutes on weekdays—a small reversal of the baseline pattern, based on only four weekend nights.

Daily steps stayed near 8,000 (8,008 versus 8,039), while active time increased modestly from 55.2 to 57.8 minutes, remaining at 21:00–22:00. Low movement barely changed: 452 versus 450 minutes, in daytime blocks of roughly 44–47 minutes separated by five-minute gaps.

Resting heart rate stayed within 55–57 bpm, averaging 55.9 versus 56.2. RMSSD averaged 40 ms in both periods; its fluctuations narrowed from 26–54 to 28–52 ms, with smaller weekend fluctuations. Activity had little relationship with the following night's sleep (r=−0.14), and heart rate and RMSSD were only weakly related. All metrics were recorded throughout.

Your sleep became repeatedly shorter and more variable: it averaged 441 versus 471 minutes over your preceding 28 days. Six nights recorded 385–392 minutes, interspersed with returns to 474–485 minutes; this occurred across weekdays and weekends, rather than as a steady decline. Wake time remained 07:00.

The timing relationship is striking: all six 90-minute activity sessions at 20:30–22:00 preceded sleep starting at 00:08–00:15 and ending the next morning, lasting 385–392 minutes. All seven observed nights after 45-minute sessions at 17:30–18:15 lasted 474–485 minutes, starting at 22:35–22:46. This strong association (r=−1.00 across 13 pairs) was absent at baseline and does not establish causation; activity intensity is unknown.

Active time averaged 64 versus 56 minutes, while steps rose only 1.8% to 8,088. Low movement stayed near 449 minutes; resting heart rate and RMSSD remained close to baseline at 56.4 bpm and 45.7 ms. Nothing was missing. Tracking whether this timing pattern repeats would be useful.

Your heart measurements showed two separate four-day changes, followed by returns to baseline. Resting heart rate rose to 65–67 bpm on April 3–6, compared with your usual 55–57, then returned to 55–57 on April 7–12. RMSSD remained at 44–47 ms during that rise, but fell to 23–26 ms on April 7–10 versus a baseline of 43–47, returning to 45 ms on April 11–12.

These changes did not overlap. The overall averages—heart rate 58.7 versus 56.0 bpm and RMSSD 38.9 versus 45.0 ms—therefore obscure their timing and subsequent recovery. The lower weekday RMSSD average reflects the April 7–10 episode; weekend values stayed near baseline.

Sleep remained around 470 minutes, starting near 22:50 and ending at 07:00, with little weekday/weekend difference. Steps and active time also stayed near baseline at 7,996 and 55 minutes; low movement decreased slightly from 451 to 447 minutes. Evening activity showed little relationship with subsequent sleep. All measurements were present. Monitor whether either temporary heart-measure change recurs.

You recorded a sustained increase in sleep throughout March 30–April 12: every night lasted 442–457 minutes, compared with 322–338 minutes across your preceding 28 days. Average sleep rose from 5 hours 28 minutes to 7 hours 28 minutes (+120 minutes, 36%). Sleep started about two hours earlier, around 23:12 instead of 01:12, while waking stayed fixed at 07:00. The increase held across weekdays and weekends, with a small further upward trend within the window.

Other measures remained close to baseline: active time averaged 55.4 versus 55.1 minutes, still around 21:00; low movement averaged 450 versus 448 minutes. Resting heart rate stayed at 55–57 bpm and RMSSD at 43–47 ms, without a corresponding sustained shift.

Steps averaged 7,963 versus 8,044, but declined within the window. Weekend steps fell from 8,195 to 7,784, while weekday steps were slightly higher at 8,035 versus 7,984. Activity had little relationship with the following night's sleep (r=0.07), so it does not explain the sleep increase. All metrics were recorded throughout.
